For exoplanets of similar composition, density increases with mass due to gravitational compression. Earth's mean density is roughly 5.5 g/cm³.

- Option a: Earth's mass and radius → density ≈ 5.5 g/cm³.
- Option b: Density explicitly ≈ 5.5 g/cm³.
- Option c: Same composition as Earth but 5 times more massive → compression yields density > 5.5 g/cm³.
- Option d: Same composition but half Earth's mass → less compression yields density < 5.5 g/cm³.

Thus, option c has the highest density.

Answer: A

d) A planet with the same composition as Earth but half the mass of Earth.

Option c: Same composition as Earth but 5 times more massive than Earth. Since composition is the same but more massive, the planet will compress due to gravity, so its density will be higher than Earth's density. For rocky planets, density increases with mass due to compression. Earth's density is ~5.5 g/cm^3, a planet with same composition but 5 times the mass will have density > 5.5 g/cm^3. This is known: super-Earths with similar composition have higher densities.

Option d: Same composition as Earth but half the mass of Earth. Lower mass means less compression, so density will be lower than Earth's density. So density < 5.5 g/cm^3.
